==English==

===Alternative forms===
* {{alter|en|speach||obsolete}}

===Etymology===
{{etymon|en|:inh|enm:speche<ety:inh<ang:spǣċ<ety:from<ang:sprǣċ>>>>|tree=1}}
From {{inh|en|enm|speche}}, from {{inh|en|ang|spǣċ}}, {{m|ang|sprǣċ||speech, discourse, language}}, from {{inh|en|gmw-pro|*sprāku||speech, language}}, from {{der|en|ine-pro|*spereg-}}, {{m|ine-pro|*spreg-||to make a sound}}. Cognate with {{cog|nl|spraak||speech}}, {{cog|de|Sprache||language, speech}}. More at {{l|en|speak}}.

===Pronunciation===
* {{IPA|en|/spiːt͡ʃ/}}
** {{audio|en|en-us-speech.ogg|a=US}}
** {{rhymes|en|iːtʃ|s=1}}
* {{IPA|en|/spiːt͡ʃ/|/spɛːt͡ʃ/|a=Early Modern}}<ref>{{R:enm:HGES|II|481|557}}</ref>

===Noun===
{{wp}}
{{en-noun|~}}

# {{lb|en|uncountable}} The ability to [[speak]]; the faculty of uttering [[word]]s or articulate [[sound]]s and [[vocalizations]] to [[communicate]].
#: {{ux|en|He had a bad '''speech''' impediment.}}
#: {{ux|en|After the accident she lost her '''speech'''.}}
#* {{RQ:Maxwell Mirror and the Lamp|chapter=12|passage=All this was extraordinarily distasteful to Churchill. It was ugly, gross. Never before had he felt such repulsion when the vicar displayed his characteristic bluntness or coarseness of '''speech'''. In the present connexion{{nb...}} such talk had been distressingly out of place.}}
#* {{RQ:Wodehouse Jeeves in the Offing|chapter=XV and XVIII|passage=I was at liberty to attend to Wilbert, who I could see desired '''speech''' with me. {{...}} As far as Bobbie and I were concerned, silence reigned, this novel twist in the scenario having wiped '''speech''' from our lips, as the expression is, but Phyllis continued vocal. {{...}}<!--ch. XVIII--> For perhaps a quarter of a minute after he had passed from the scene the aged relative stood struggling for utterance. At the end of this period she found '''speech'''. “Of all the damn silly fatheaded things!”}}
# {{lb|en|uncountable}} The act of speaking, a certain style of it.
#: {{syn|en|Thesaurus:speech}}
#: {{ux|en|It was hard to hear his '''speech''' over the noise.}}
#: {{ux|en|Her '''speech''' was soft and lilting.}}
#* {{RQ:Economist|date=2014-04-21|volume=411|issue=8884
|url=http://www.economist.com/news/science-and-technology/21601233-exploring-link-between-manganese-and-parkinsons-disease-subtle-effects|title=Subtle effects
|passage=Manganism has been known about since the 19th century, when miners exposed to ores containing manganese, a silvery metal, began to totter, slur their '''speech''' and behave like someone inebriated.|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20140430162808/http://www.economist.com/news/science-and-technology/21601233-exploring-link-between-manganese-and-parkinsons-disease-subtle-effects}}
# {{senseid|en|oration}}{{lb|en|countable}} A formal session of [[speak]]ing, especially a long oral message given publicly by one person.
#: {{syn|en|address|id1=speech|allocution|monologue|oration|soliloquy}}
#: {{ux|en|The candidate made some ambitious promises in his campaign '''speech'''.}}
#* {{quote-book|en|year=1720|author=w:Jonathan Swift|title=[[s:The Works of the Rev. Jonathan Swift/Volume 5/A Letter to a Young Clergyman|A Letter to a Young Clergyman]]
|passage=The constant design of both these orators, in all their '''speeches''', was to drive some one particular point.}}
#* {{RQ:Wodehouse Jeeves in the Offing|chapter=I and XII|passage=He's going to present the prizes at Market Snodsbury Grammar School. We've been caught short as usual, and somebody has got to make a '''speech''' on ideals and the great world outside to those blasted boys, so he fits in nicely. I believe he's a very fine speaker. His only trouble is that he's stymied unless he has his '''speech''' with him and can read it. Calls it referring to his notes. {{...}}<!--ch. XII--> “So that's why he's been going about looking like a dead fish. I suppose Roberta broke the engagement?” “In a '''speech''' lasting five minutes without a pause for breath.”}}
# {{lb|en|countable}} A [[dialect]], [[vernacular]], or {{lb|en|dated}} a [[language]].
#: {{syn|en|Thesaurus:language}}
#* {{RQ:KJV|Ezekiel|3|6|passage=For thou art not sent to a people of a strange '''speech''', and of an hard language, but to the house of Israel.}}
#* {{quote-book|en|title=The Fyrst Boke of the Introduction of Knowledge|author=w:Andrew Boorde|year=1542|passage=The '''speche''' of Englande is a base '''speche''' to other noble '''speches''', as Italion, Castylion, and Frenche; howbeit the '''speche''' of Englande of late dayes is amended.}}
# {{lb|en|uncountable}} Language used [[orally]], rather than in writing.
#: {{ux|en|This word is mostly used in '''speech'''.}}
# {{lb|en|grammar}} An utterance that is [[quote]]d; ''see'' {{m|en|direct speech}}, {{m|en|reported speech}}
# {{lb|en|uncountable}} Public [[talk]], [[news]], [[gossip]], [[rumour]].
#* {{RQ:Shakespeare Henry 8|I|iii|passage=The duke{{...}}did of me demand / What was the '''speech''' among the Londoners / Concerning the French journey.}}

===Verb===
{{en-verb}}

# {{lb|en|transitive|intransitive}} To [[make]] (a [[#Noun|speech]]); to [[harangue]].
#* {{RQ:Swift Works|volume=VII|title=Orator against Peace|page=73|passage=I'll '''speech''' against peace while Dismal's my name, / And be a true whig, while I'm Not-in-game.}}
#* {{quote-book
|en
|year=1731
|title=The Statesman: A New Court Ballad
|pageurl=https://books.google.co.uk/books?id=cRRlAAAAcAAJ&pg=PA7
|page=7
|passage=So to '''Speeching''' he did go, / And like a Man of Senſe, / He certainly ſaid Ay or No,
}}
#* {{RQ:NYT|date=11 June 1905|title=Cheer Battery Dan at Lawyers’ Recption{{nb...|Magistrate Finn Listens to Flowery and Flattering Addresses. 57 Varieties of Speeches; Members of the Supreme Court, Essex Market, and Battery Bars All Join in Friendly Tributes.}}|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1905/06/11/archives/cheer-battery-dan-at-lawyers-reception-magistrate-finn-listens-to.html|volume=LIV|issue=17,305|page=6|pageurl=https://archive.org/details/sim_new-york-times_1905-06-11_54_17305/page/n5/mode/1up|column=3|passage=Two lawyers who had come over from Williamsburg to make speeches in honor of Battery Dan were told by Lawyer William J. Caffrey that only Manhattanites would be allowed to speak. “If you let my friend '''speech''' something,” said one of the Williamsburgers, “I will be satisfactioned mitout{{sic}} '''speeching'''.{{nb...}}”}}
#* {{quote-journal
|en
|date=1965-06
|volume=127
|number=6
|title=Wales, Land of Bards
|journal=w:National Geographic
|passage="He wasn't one to make himself big," said Mr. Jones. "But he had something that drew the people when he was '''speeching'''... When he came down we all used to shout 'Lloyd George am byth!' You know, 'Lloyd George forever!' That was just how we felt."
}}
